learn.title: let, make and have + person + base verb
learn.html:
These three verbs are used to talk about permission, obligations and orders. After them comes object + base form of the verb (without to).

VerbMeaningExample
let + object + baseallow, permitMy parents won't let me stay out late.
make + object + baseforce, make someone do somethingThey make me come home before 10:00.
have + object + baseask for, arrange (more neutral)I have them do their homework before dinner.

Watch the meaning: make sounds like a strong obligation (My boss makes us work on Saturdays); have is softer and more normal (I have my assistant send the emails); let means giving permission. In the negative: They don't let me…. With object pronouns, use me, you, him, her, us, them.

watch.wrong: My parents don't let me to stay out late.
watch.right: My parents don't let me stay out late.
watch.why: After let + object comes the base verb, without to.

watch.wrong: My mom makes me to clean my room.
watch.right: My mom makes me clean my room.
watch.why: Make + object + base verb, without to.

watch.wrong: She makes that I wash the dishes.
watch.right: She makes me wash the dishes.
watch.why: English doesn't use a subjunctive here: object + base verb.

watch.wrong: I have my kids to do their homework.
watch.right: I have my kids do their homework.
watch.why: Have + object + base verb, without to.

learn.title: get, want, ask, tell and help + person + to + verb
learn.html:
With these verbs, the object is followed by to + verb. It is a very different structure from Spanish, which uses a subjunctive clause after the verb.

VerbExample
get + object + to + verb (persuade)I can't get them to clean up their rooms.
want + object + to + verbMy parents want me to study law.
ask + object + to + verbI have to ask them to drive me everywhere.
tell + object + to + verbMy wife is always telling me to slow down.
help + object + (to) + verbMy kids never help me (to) clean the house.

With help, you can use the base verb or to + verb, but the form without to is more common. In the negative: I told her not to worry.

watch.wrong: My dad wants that I study law.
watch.right: My dad wants me to study law.
watch.why: Want + object + to + verb; there is no “want that + subject”.

I asked him to help me.

learn.title: used to and would: past habits and situations
learn.html:
To talk about things that happened regularly in the past and no longer happen (in Spanish, the imperfect tense), there are two options.

UseFormExample
Past habitsused to + base, or would / 'd + baseI used to go / I'd go to my sister's house a lot.
Situations or states that are no longer trueonly used to + baseMy sister used to live next door.
Negativedidn't use to + baseI didn't use to like jazz.
QuestionDid + subject + use to + base?What kind of music did you use to like?

Key rule: would only works for repeated actions (we would play cards every Sunday), not for states such as live, have, be, like. In negatives and questions you write use to (without -d), because did already marks the past.

Don't confuse used to + verb (a past habit) with be used to + -ing (to be accustomed to something).

watch.wrong: I use to play outside every day.
watch.right: I used to play outside every day.
watch.why: In the affirmative, write used to (with -d).

watch.wrong: She didn't used to eat meat.
watch.right: She didn't use to eat meat.
watch.why: After didn't comes use to, without -d.

watch.wrong: When I was a kid, I would have a dog.
watch.right: When I was a kid, I used to have a dog.
watch.why: Have here is a state, not a repeated action: only used to.

watch.wrong: We used to going to the beach.
watch.right: We used to go to the beach.

learn.title: Writing: time markers (past and present)
learn.html:
To contrast the past with the present when writing, use time markers and keep the correct verb tense.

For the pastFor the present
When we were kids, … / When I was younger, …
In those days, … / Back then, …		Today, … / Now, … / Nowadays, … / These days, …
When I was younger, my sister and I used to roller-skate a lot.Nowadays, kids wear a lot of safety equipment.

If the marker is at the start, write a comma after it. At the end you don't need one: Kids wear helmets nowadays. Combine the two tenses to contrast: Back then, we didn't have safety equipment, but nowadays kids wear it.

watch.wrong: Back then, I am very shy.
watch.right: Back then, I was very shy.
watch.why: Back then marks the past: was.

watch.wrong: Nowadays, we used to talk by video call.
watch.right: Nowadays, we talk by video call.
watch.why: Nowadays marks the present: simple present.

watch.wrong: When I was a kid I have a bike.
watch.right: When I was a kid, I had a bike.
watch.why: After when I was… comes a past verb (had / used to have).

learn.title: Strategy: giving opinions and showing agreement
learn.html:
To give an opinion:

  • I think … — I think people should get more time off.
  • I don't think … — I don't think we get enough time together. (In English, the negative goes on think, not on the second verb.)
  • It seems like … — It seems like we don't get enough time to relax.
  • It seems to me (that) … — It seems to me that people don't spend enough time with their families.
  • If you ask me, … — If you ask me, we all work too much these days.

To show agreement: Absolutely. / Definitely. / Exactly. / You're right. / That's true. / That's for sure. / I agree (with you). / (Oh,) yeah. / (Oh,) I know.

A: If you ask me, we all work too much these days. B: Absolutely.

learn.title: Useful expressions
learn.html:
• My parents won't let me stay out late. — talking about permission and limits.
  • They make me come home before 10:00. — talking about obligations.
  • I can't get them to clean up their rooms. — family frustration.
  • My parents want me to study law. — other people's expectations.
  • I used to … / We'd … when we were kids. — remembering childhood.
  • If you ask me, … / It seems to me that … — giving your opinion.
  • Absolutely. / That's for sure. / I know. — showing agreement.
  • I have a gripe about … — complaining about something.

write.prompt: Write a text (120 to 180 words) about your childhood: what your family was like, what you used to do (used to / would), and what rules there were at home (let, make, want). Opening example: When I was a kid, I used to live with my grandparents…
checklist: Between 120 and 180 words
At least 3 sentences with used to or would (no mistakes with -d or -ing)
One sentence with let or make + base verb
One sentence with want / ask / tell + object + to + verb
Markers such as when I was…, back then, in those days, followed by a comma
At least 3 family words
write.model:
When I was a kid, I used to live with my grandparents in a small town. My parents worked in the city, so they only came home on weekends. My grandmother used to cook delicious meals, and my grandfather would tell me stories every night before bed. Back then, we didn't have a computer, so I would play outside with my cousins all afternoon.

My grandparents were strict, but they were also kind. They let me watch cartoons after I did my homework. They didn't let me stay up late, and they made me clean my room every Saturday. My grandmother always wanted me to eat all my vegetables, and my grandfather told me to be polite to everyone. In those days, I thought their rules were boring, but now I understand them.

I also had a little brother and an older sister. My sister used to help me with my homework, and my brother would follow me everywhere. In summer, my mother used to take us to the beach.

write.prompt: Write an opinion text (120 to 180 words): do children today have more or fewer rules and pressure than in the past? Compare the past with the present, give at least three opinions, and mention one point that another person would agree with. Opening example: If you ask me, kids today have a lot of pressure…
checklist: Between 120 and 180 words
If you ask me / It seems to me that / I think / I don't think
Past–present contrast with back then and nowadays
One agreement expression (Absolutely, That's for sure)
One example with let / make / have
Verbs in the correct tense after each marker
write.model:
If you ask me, kids today have a lot of pressure. Back then, when I was a child, we used to play in the street until it was dark, and our parents didn't worry much. Nowadays, children have more homework and fewer free hours than in the past. It seems to me that many of them are always tired.

I don't think that technology is all bad, but I think it makes children's lives more stressful. In the past, our parents didn't let us watch TV before we finished our homework, and they made us go to bed at eight o'clock. Today, parents let their kids use phones and tablets for hours. Some parents also have very high expectations, so they make their children take extra classes every afternoon.

I think the rules of the past were stricter, but they were also simpler. Nowadays, kids have to be good at school, sports and music at the same time. A friend of mine says, "Children should have more time to play." Absolutely! That's for sure.

reading.title: Summers at my grandmother's house
reading.intro: Read Rosa's text about her childhood and answer the questions.
paragraphs: When I was a kid, I used to spend every summer at my grandmother's house in a small town near Guadalajara. My parents worked a lot, so my brother Pablo, my cousin Lucía and I stayed with her for two months. Back then, I thought it was the best place in the world, and now I think so, too.

My grandmother was strict, but she was also very kind. She made us get up at seven, and she made us clean our rooms before breakfast. She didn't let us watch TV until the afternoon. Her rule was simple: first chores, then fun. I used to gripe about it all the time, and Lucía and Pablo would fight over the remote every night.

Every morning, my grandfather would ask us to help him in the garden. We would water the plants and pick fruit, and he never told us to hurry. Sometimes my grandmother got us to help her make tortillas, and she would tell stories about when she was young. In those days, she said, there was no electricity in her village, and children walked two hours to school.

Nowadays, things are very different. Kids have cell phones and tablets, and many of them don't spend much time outside. If you ask me, children today have a lot of pressure and too little free time. My nephew, for example, has classes every afternoon. It seems to me that families don't eat together as much as they used to. My mother agrees. "That's for sure," she says.

Last year, my grandmother turned ninety. The whole family came over for dinner, even my uncle from Chicago and my sister-in-law with her twins. We cooked her recipes and looked at old photos. I really want my own kids to have the same memories someday. I'm going to ask them to spend a summer there, and I hope my grandmother will let them help in the kitchen.
